#8239. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”

#8237. ‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

Published Nov 16, 2026 2:00 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

For three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer. They kept tabs on the buck with trail cameras and debated when it was time to shoot the high and wide whitetail.

“We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life. “Over last summer when he was still in velvet we saw on cameras that his rack had completely blown up and got huge, with lots of palmation.”

It was clear this was the season to try to kill him. The brothers hunted hard during a 23-day stint in October, with one of them in a stand every day.

“I was just the lucky one sitting that day when the buck slipped up,” says Zack, a business-studies student at Louisiana Tech University. “My brother, dad, and I put in a lot of work hunting that buck. I would not have taken this deer without their help.”

The Halberts had multiple setups around their 80-acre hunting property. Zack took the buck from a ground blind on a 48-degree morning in late October.

“The blind faced the woods, and I’m looking one way out a window, then leaned the other way, and there he was at 21 yards,” Zack says. “It’s crazy how you can go from calm and in two seconds go into full panic mode.”

Zack watched the buck for three long minutes as he waited for a broadside shot. When the buck finally turned, he drew and held at full draw for about 15 seconds. Then he let fly.

The buck took off, and Zack watched where it disappeared into the woods. Then he called his brother, dad, and girlfriend with the news.

“When I shot I was so pumped I almost shook the ground blind over. Before I got out of the blind I was trying to stop shaking enough to finish my prayer for what a blessing it was.”

Zack began trailing the deer into timber, but the blood became faint and he decided it would be best to call in a tracking dog.

“I didn’t want to mess up on this deer,” he says.

Tracker Eric Perry and his dog, Blue, arrived that evening.

“It was getting toward dusk when the dog got there and was put on the buck’s trail,” Zack says. “Blue found it in just 15 minutes. The arrow was a good hit, but there was no exit hole and so not a good blood trail.”

The deer had died in a creek, and Zack had to wade into the cold water to get his buck out. The crew dragged the deer out of the timber and loaded it into a truck and headed home. Zack estimates it was 5½ years old, and Buckmasters scorer Chris Bates measured Zack’s buck at 205 3/8 inches.

Although Buckmasters has a different scoring system than the one used by Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young Clubs (and therefore scores aren’t apples-to-apples), it’s worth noting that the largest nontypical killed with a bow in the state scored, according to P&Y records, 206 5/8 inches. That deer was taken in January 2012 by Alton McLead.

Read Next: No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck

“I know my grandpa Dan, who isn’t with us anymore,” says Zack, “wouldn’t have believed his eyes if he got to see this deer.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8235. Alaska Considers ‘Unprecedented’ Closure of Public Land to Hunting, Trapping Along Controversial Ambler Road

Published Nov 16, 2026 4:38 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road. The decision would be part of a push by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority to build a road creating private access to a future mining district focused on copper and zinc deposits.

While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat issues, the recent development is creating even more consternation.

“It’s unprecedented,” says Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. “We’re supposed to allow for balanced use of all of our resources. This would show preference to one resource over another.”

The proposal, which the Alaska Board of Game will consider during an online meeting Friday, would close 1 mile on either side of the 211-mile proposed road in northern Alaska to all hunting and trapping. It first became public in February and is part of a memorandum of understanding between several Alaskan native corporations and the state. The proposed closure is part of a “subsistence safeguard,” according to a story in the Alaska Beacon. Subsistence hunters could still cross through the road corridor to access other legal hunting grounds.

The hunting and trapping ban would begin July 1, 2029, and remain in place through at least Jan. 1, 2036, regardless of when or even if the road is built, Glaves says.

The Board of Game considered formalizing the MOU in a July meeting, and opposition was fierce, says Glaves. Still, many Alaskan organizations could not prepare comment because the meeting was in the middle of fishing season. As a result, the board tabled the discussion until its formal meeting in January.

A few months later, the Alaska Fish and Game commissioner announced another special meeting Nov. 20 to discuss the project, allowing only written public comment and no oral testimony.

“That isn’t illegal,” Glaves says, “but it’s not in the best interest of engaging the public.”

Even more importantly, if the closure passes, it tells Alaskans that state public land can be shut down to access at the request of an anticipated industry and with no stated biological need.

The road has not been built, and there’s some question about whether or not Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democratic governor-elect, will support the project. He has not stated a position publicly but has said he will carefully evaluate money spent by the state. The Industrial Development and Export Authority, an economic development arm of the state, would be responsible for building the road. The Alaska Wilderness League, which opposes the project, estimates it could cost the state more than $2 billion including construction, maintenance, and financing.

The preemptive nature of the closure is particularly troubling to conservation groups.

Read Next: The Ambler Road Project Would Jeopardize One of the Last Great Wilderness Hunts in America

“There is no compelling reason to establish these restrictions years before the project is constructed or in the absence of demonstrated need,” she wrote on Nov. 4. “Doing so would also set a troubling precedent of using the Board’s time and public resources to evaluate hypothetical impacts of projects that may never materialize, rather than addressing actual wildlife management and public access concerns as they arise.”

Christine Peterson is a freelance writer based in southeast Wyoming covering hunting, fishing, outdoor recreation, wildlife and the environment for Outdoor Life, High Country News, National Geographic and others.

#8233. 2027 Winter Gear Guide: The Best Skis, Boots, and Outerwear of the Season

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

A SKI Test at Deer Valley, a boot test on Mount Hood, and 430 days testing ski pants later, this is the ski gear worth the money. (Photo: Re Wikstrom)

A skier’s fall ritual: taking inventory of the gear closet. What stays, what goes? The jacket survived another season, the boots are fine as long as nobody asks questions, and the goggles might be saved by a new lens. Eventually, something has to be replaced, and everything on the ski shop racks has a marketing pitch. The 2027 Winter Gear Guide is our case for what’s actually worth the money.

Our men’s ski pants testers alone logged 430 ski days last season, which is a lot of time to find out whether a pant seat is truly waterproof. Spread that scrutiny across skis, boots, outerwear, and accessories and you get the 2027 Winter Gear Guide: more than 400 products, a SKI Test at Deer Valley, and a ski boot test on Mount Hood (50 pairs, 10 testers, two weeks).

Of those more than 400 products, 20 earned highest honors. Best in Test is reserved for the winners of SKI Test, our annual ski shootout at Deer Valley, where each ski goes head to head with a full category field and comes out on top. Editors’ Choice goes to gear that brought new tech that changes how well the product works, proved themselves season after season, or surprised us in a category where nobody saw it coming. Best Overall is the simplest: the product that tested better than anything else in its category.

If you’re on the hunt for new gear this season and only the best will do, start here. Each pick links to its full roundup, where you can see how it stacks up against the competition and read the cons—we always have cons.

Few skis have defined a category like the Enforcer. At 99 millimeters underfoot, it’s built for skiers who attack the whole mountain, from refrozen groomers to chopped-up afternoon snow. Its heft keeps it calm where lighter skis get bounced around, and edge grip on firm snow is a standout. The tradeoff is effort: it rewards sharp technique, floats less well than its width suggests, and can feel like work in bumps. Expect a driver’s ski. Read the full review.

Women who spend more time off the groomers than on them will find a willing partner in the M-Pro W 98. At 98 millimeters, it moves between corduroy and off-piste chunder without hesitation, and its stability builds confidence when speed climbs. It’s a directional, big-mountain-leaning ski, which means it asks for strength and a committed stance. Lighter or less aggressive skiers may find it beefy. For rippers who want one ski to charge anywhere, it delivers. Read the full women’s all-mountain ski guide.

The M-Free 108 won Best in Test without winning a single performance category, a reminder that consistency beats flash. Testers found it versatile enough to cover a wide range of terrain, and it floats like a ski much wider than its 108-millimeter waist. That makes it a smart pick for freeride-minded skiers who want one pair for storm days and everything in between, rather than a specialist that shines in only one condition. Read the full review.

Where some wide skis chase fun, the Santa Ana 102 chases speed. It stays calm through chopped-up snow and meets every snow type with energy, as long as the skier can match it. That’s the catch: lesser-skilled skiers may find it unforgiving, it’s stiff in bumps, and driving it takes real leg strength. For strong skiers who want a 102-millimeter ski that rewards commitment and holds its line when the going gets tough, it’s the benchmark. Read the full review.

The Mantra name has long meant power, and the 88 shrinks that formula into a frontside ski. Testers praised how smoothly it rolls from one edge to the other, with a responsiveness closer to a race ski than most frontside designs. It’s stiff and demanding, and the tip can deflect when snow gets cut up, so it’s happiest on groomed and firm terrain. Pick it if you ski fast, ski hard, and want a precise tool. Read the full review.

If you want a frontside ski that takes the guesswork out of starting a turn, the Arcade W 88 is it. A big tip pulls you into an arc intuitively, and it handles groomers, bumps, and mixed snow with equal composure. It wants to stay on edge, so it’s not the choice for sideways, slarvy fun. Skiers who prefer a grippy, predictable ride across changing conditions will find a trustworthy everyday partner here. Read the full review.

Carving skis have drifted wider and friendlier, but the Montero AX still feels like race ski’s cousin. With an 80-millimeter waist, it tips onto edge with little effort and stays planted at speed, rewarding skiers who drive it with intent. The price is steep, and less assertive skiers may find it unforgiving. If you live for corduroy and want a ski you can trust when the speedometer climbs, this is the one. Read the full review.

Powder skis can be lively or powerful, rarely both. The Antimatter 114 manages it. Generous rocker at the tip and tail plus a 114-millimeter waist keep it on top of deep snow, while the ski still feels energetic when you hit it hard. It’s a lot of ski for intermediates and comes only in long lengths, and a few testers noticed some wobble in a straight line at full speed. Expert-leaning powder hounds will love it. Read the full review.

Armada’s Locator 112 is a touring ski with a soft-snow personality. At 1,575 grams per ski, testers found it exceptionally playful in powder. It gives up some reliability on firm snow and isn’t the most nimble in tight terrain, so it’s best matched to big, open lines and storm-day objectives rather than icy couloirs. Choose it when your plan is untracked snow and a lively ride. Read the full review.

A liner refresh, not a redesign, keeps the Shadow MV on top. It suits skiers who equate comfort with a precise, snug fit rather than extra room, with a 100-millimeter last and a progressive flex that transfers power straight to the ski. Testers liked the shin fit and flex feel, and the liner’s design helps avoid pressure points. It runs slightly short, so size carefully. Read the full review.

Tecnica’s Mach 1 is a perennial favorite in SKI’s boot tests, and the women’s TD2 version earns Editors’ Choice by being easier to live with. It’s simpler to get on than past generations, fits a broad range of foot and leg shapes, and delivers a quick, snappy flex that translates to rapid edge response. On fit: Ankle pockets may bite at first. Read the full review.

The Radical Pro is a midweight touring boot that doesn’t feel like a compromise. At 1,400 grams, it offers a remarkably free 60-degree range of motion for climbing, then stiffens progressively as you flex forward for the descent. Fit is generous through a wide last, which suits many feet but may feel cavernous on narrow ones. For backcountry skiers who need one boot to handle long approaches and confident skiing, it makes a strong case. Read the full review.

Raide’s TourTech is a shell built for people who earn their turns. It breathes well when you’re working hard on the skin track, packs down small enough to stash when the sun comes out, and carries thoughtful backcountry touches. The tradeoff of a shell is warmth: on the coldest storm days you’ll need to layer underneath. It isn’t cheap, but for women who tour more than they lap lifts, it earns its Editors’ Choice. Read the full review.

Fit is the whole argument for the Bigline Bib. The cut has plenty of room for puffy long underwear, but three adjustment points (waist cinches, long suspenders, hem buttons) snug it down so nothing drags or sags. A soft three-layer Pertex Shield outer reliably deflected soggy Pacific Northwest storms. Thigh pockets swallow a skin each, so slackcountry laps are covered. These are uninsulated, so be sure to layer up for cold days. Read the full review.

Testers had a hard time finding fault with the Chariot Primo, which is a rarity among women’s ski pants. Its hybrid fit is relaxed enough to layer and move in without getting baggy, and short, regular, and tall inseams let you skip the tailor. Three-layer PNW Primo fabric offers 20,000 millimeters of waterproofing, and TechSteel kick patches guard the cuffs. With no insulation, you’ll need to layer for the weather, but we love these bibs’ versatility. Read the full review

A former Editors’ Choice winner, the Defiant Shell takes the best all-around honor among men’s jackets on comfort, weather protection, and smart details. Venting is excellent, the pocket layout is generous, and the double front zipper is a thoughtful touch. In stormier conditions, its proprietary membrane kept wet, heavy flakes from soaking through. It’s uninsulated, so you control warmth with layers. Read the full review.

Salomon’s Skarn Prime earns the overall nod in the goggles category by doing a lot well. A toric lens gives an expansive field of view, the face foam is layered three deep, and the magnetic lens swap is quick and intuitive. It also pairs with a wide range of helmets. The catches are fit and price: it’s sized large, so smaller faces may swim in it, and $295 is steep. If it fits your face, it’s the one to beat. Read the full review.

Sweet Protection’s Switcher 2Vi MIPS took the overall helmet title on comfort, goggle compatibility, and airflow. The Occigrip turn-dial makes fit adjustments quick, and the 2Vi platform and MIPS layer handle impact protection. Venting is excellent, which helps when the temperature climbs. The only real complaint was bulky ear pads. At 560 grams and $300, it’s not the lightest or cheapest lid, but it covers a lot of ground with few compromises. Read the full review.

Rab’s Guide GTX Gauntlets give you protection without bulk. A Gore-Tex Active shell keeps weather out, 100-gsm PrimaLoft Gold and a high-pile lining supply the warmth, and the low-profile cuff tucks over or under a jacket sleeve cleanly. They’re built to last through a hard season, and Rab also offers an undercuff glove and a mitten version if the gauntlet isn’t your style. At $170, they’re a smart, do-it-all pick. Read the full review.

Swany’s Nexus leans on a new heating platform called ewool and 22-watt-hour batteries, and the result is heat that lasts: up to eight hours on low, four on normal, three on high. Testers liked the haptic feedback when changing settings, the high-quality leather, and that you can charge without pulling the batteries out. A mitt version is also offered for the coldest hands. At $480 it’s an investment, but it’s the heated glove to beat. Read the full review.

#8232. The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

Published Nov 16, 2026 6:13 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

This story, “I Shot Big Red,” appeared in the January 1967 issue of Outdoor Life. Shelton’s buck is now the 20th biggest typical whitetail ever taken in Kentucky, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. At the time, however, it was the biggest ever taken in Kentucky. It also had a wider inside and outside spread than any deer on the books, including the then-world-record deer.

At 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime. The rain, which had been steady since before dawn, suddenly stopped, and the woods of northern Todd County, Kentucky, were still. I was 20 feet up in a huge sycamore, watching a deer runway that meandered through thick brush. I’d been half-wet most of the day, and I felt another case of chills coming on.

I might as well quit, I thought. I’m not going to see Big Red, and I probably won’t see any other deer.

My thoughts seemed logical, but another line of reasoning wouldn’t be denied. This was Todd County’s first deer season in modern times, and the season was for this day only. So far as Big Red was concerned, I had good reason to believe he was the best trophy whitetail buck in North America. Besides, I’m mighty stubborn when it comes to deer hunting. I decided to stay in that tree till dark.

In front of me, to the north and 30 yards away, a tiny creek flowed through a heavily wooded east-west valley. The runway crossed the creek and continued into dense thickets. I couldn’t see the thickets’ far edge, but I knew the growth thinned against a hillside that topped out alongside a stubble cornfield 200 yards away. The cornfield was 40 yards wide and bordered a little-used gravel road. Across the road was 40 acres of tangled cedars, the thickest cover in the area. I figured any deer leaving those cedars would use the runway I was watching.

Around 2:30 a twig snapped behind me, to the south. Then I heard branches rubbing together and sounds resembling a squirrel digging in the ground. I knew I was listening to a deer.

The sounds were a few yards off the runway. In another minute they became more distinguishable, and I knew the animal was working toward me. I had two choices: remain motionless in hopes the deer would move past me, or try to inch my way around so I’d face south.

Though the leaves were off the trees, I figured I had an excellent chance of moving without being seen. I was standing on a huge branch, but I was tight against the trunk. Deer don’t normally look up, so I also had that advantage. In addition, I figured the deer was feeding and not alerted to immediate danger. I moved as cautiously as possible.

It took a few minutes to make my move. Now I was facing south. Surprisingly, I could still hear the same sounds, but I couldn’t see any movement.

The sounds kept coming closer. Then, as if by magic, there he was. I saw antlers and legs at the same instant, about 30 yards away. The buck was pawing at acorns. I couldn’t get a clear view of his antlers, and I didn’t dare risk a shot through that thick brush. There wasn’t much I could do except wait.

After what seemed like hours, he suddenly tossed his head up. He seemed to be looking straight at me. His rack was massive, but I knew instantly it didn’t belong to Big Red. I was sure the buck had caught a glimpse of me or winded me.

I better take him, I thought. Time is running out.

My .44 Magnum Ruger carbine was braced against the trunk. I started lining the crosswires of my Weaver scope on his chest. Then, through my variable-power scope, I made an amazing discovery. That buck wasn’t looking up at me at all; he was staring on the level along the runway toward the north.

Now the eight-pointer relaxed and dropped his head to feed again. I heard the same sounds that had startled him. To the north, behind me now, I heard another deer. I glanced over my shoulder and got the second biggest shock of my life. Big Red, in all his glory, was walking toward my tree stand. The monstrous buck was in clear view, 50 yards away and moving down the runway. There was no question about his identity.

I had seen him two years ago when we had come face to face under the most dramatic conditions. We had startled each other that time. Now I had all the cards. Or did I? I was in no position to shoot. If that buck was alerted to the slightest suspicion, he’d bound into the thickets and disappear.

This dream situation had been in the making for a long time. I guess it really started when I was nine years old, the day I shot my first squirrel. After stalking the gray for hours, I knocked it off a stump with my brother Rudy’s .22. I decided then and there I wanted to become the world’s best hunter. That boyhood ambition has never dimmed, though it’s been realistically tempered by maturity. At that time my family lived in the town of Mayfield, in southwestern Kentucky. There was plenty of small game and birds, but no deer.

By the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

By the time I was in high school, I was addicted to duck hunting. The area around Mayfield is laced with creeks, rivers, and potholes. It was a duck paradise. I taught myself how to call by sneaking up on flocks of waterfowl and listening to their various calls. I’d go hunting before and after school every day during the season. I practically lived outdoors. But by the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

I’m 26 now and live in Bowling Green, where I work as a real estate salesman and auctioneer. My wife and I have a daughter, four, and a son, two.

Kentucky’s first modern deer season opened in 1956, when I was still a teenager. I didn’t get a chance to hunt deer until 1959, but nobody ever dreamed about deer hunting more than I did.

Looking back, I realize I started my first season as quite a stupid deer hunter. I had no experience, and I’d never seen a deer in my life. The 1959 season lasted three days, and I hunted every one of them from dawn to dark. After it was all over, my record was unblemished: I still hadn’t seen a deer. I’m not sure I even saw a fresh track.

Three months before the 1960 season opened, I started scouting my hunting territory on weekends. With six weeks to go, I stepped up my scouting trips to every couple of days. I found runways and beds, examined browse conditions, and located the “use” areas of three herds of whitetails. It all paid off. I killed a fat doe from a tree stand just after dawn on the opening day of the season.

I missed the 1961 season because of a session with Uncle Sam, but I didn’t lose contact with shooting. My ability with a rifle was good enough to win me an instructor’s rating, and I had charge of an army rifle range for 10 months.

In 1962 and 1963, I collected my second and third whitetails. I shot both of them while sneaking silently into bedding areas I’d discovered on scouting trips. My 1962 deer bolted from thick brush 80 yards away, and I dropped him with a single bullet. My third deer, a six-pointer, heard me pussyfooting along, but I saw him before he spotted me. He went down in his tracks.

After I killed my first deer, I studied taxidermy and began mounting deer heads for my friends. I mounted the head of my big six-pointer, but every time I looked at it I dreamed of the day when those six points would be dwarfed by a much larger rack. My dream had plenty of substance because by this time I’d seen Big Red.

We met in October, 1962, while I was living in the town of Elkton, Todd County. I’d heard that the county might be opened to deer hunting, so I started scouting likely areas. I’d done some business with H. Sweeney, a local farmer, and he’d told me he frequently saw deer crossing his fields.

On one of my scouting trips, I found a heavily traveled runway through a hilly area of oak, poplar, hickory, and cedar. The runway was pocked with fresh tracks, and I followed it down through the hills and across a valley to where it led into a rye field. Where the field met the woods, a huge oak tree offered a perfect stand. I decided to climb the tree and see what moved along the runway toward evening.

About 5 p.m. I heard some deer coming through the woods. It was a warm, quiet day, and the trees were still in full foliage, so I heard them for a long time before I saw them. Shortly, three deer walked below me and went out into the rye field to feed. I watched them for half an hour. Then I heard another deer. He moved steadily to the last bit of cover, then stopped.

I made out the partial outline of a huge deer. The whitetail stood motionless for a full five minutes; then he stepped into the field and joined the other animals. He had an eight-point rack and was the biggest deer I’d ever seen.

Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

Then I heard dogs barking. They were chasing something, and the sounds kept coming closer. A six-point buck suddenly burst out of the woods, ran under my tree, and joined the other deer. As if on signal, they all bolted out of sight.

I never did see the dogs or any more deer, though I stayed in the tree till dusk. I’d traveled farther than I thought, and it was dark before I got halfway back to my car. I decided to bypass the woods and stay in the fields. It was this decision that set up the chance meeting with Big Red.

I was crossing a fescue field when I approached a man-made stock pond. Banks, about 10 feet high, had been bulldozed around the pond to collect and hold water. I could have walked around the embankment, but I decided to walk along the top of it. A full moon had just cleared the horizon, and the landscape was bathed with an eerie beauty. I went up to the top of the bank and got the shock of my life. Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

The huge animal was silhouetted against the moon in fantastic beauty. I guess we saw each other in the same instant, and we both froze, each sizing up the other.

I remember my breath going out in a gasp. My first thought was that I was looking at somebody’s tame elk. Then I knew the animal had to be a deer. His size didn’t awe me so much as did the tremendous spread of his antlers.

We must have stared at each other for seconds. Then the monster buck snorted, whirled, and bolted down the bank and across the field. About 75 yards away, he leaped a five-foot fence. Then he stopped and looked back. I took a few steps toward him, and he trotted into some woods.

I was talking to myself when I got back to the farmer’s yard where I’d parked my car. I went up to the house and knocked on the door. He didn’t seem very impressed when I exclaimed, “I’ve just seen the biggest buck in Kentucky!”

“That’s Big Red,” he said. “I’ve seen him a few times. You can’t mistake him. He’s a lot bigger than an ordinary deer. His face is sort of reddish. That’s why we call him Big Red. The local farmers know about him, and you’re going to have plenty of company if you figure on hunting that buck.”

As it turned out, Todd County wasn’t open for deer hunting in 1962 or 1963. Kentucky controls its whitetail population by allowing hunting only in counties where the herds have built up to the carrying capacity of available deer range. In 1956 (the first year that deer hunting had been allowed since 1911) only 27 of the state’s 120 counties were open to shooting. In that season 6,000 hunters killed 1,300 whitetails. By comparison, 14,000 hunters bagged 4,100 deer in 1965. The 1966 population was estimated at well over 50,000 deer, and hunting was allowed in 74 counties.

All of this had its beginning in 1950 when the state began its stocking program with deer bought from Pennsylvania. Original stockings were made in Mammoth Cave National Park and Federal Wildlife refuges. With a ban on hunting, these herds multiplied so rapidly that certain areas became overrun with deer. Live-trapping crews thinned out the overpopulated sections and stocked the deer in other areas that had heavy browse conditions. As these herds build to huntable populations, additional counties are opened to hunting.

In the summer of 1964, the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources announced that Todd County would have its first deer season, a one-day hunt on November 28. I told my brother Rudy about Big Red, and we planned to hunt him together. We didn’t get much sleep the night before the season opened, and we left for our hunting area at 3 a.m.

A few changes had taken place during the two years since I’d met Big Red. The monster buck had moved from the Sweeney farm to adjoining woodlands owned by farmer Ross Laster. The deer’s travel routes had also changed, but I knew all about this because I knew Ross well and hadn’t relaxed my scouting trips. I hadn’t seen the buck a second time, but I’d found his tracks many times, and some of the local farmers had seen him just a month earlier.

Dawn was breaking when Rudy and I drove down a gravel road toward Ross’s farm. A mile from our destination, a four-point buck jumped across the road ahead of us, ran to the far edge of a small stubble cornfield and stopped.

“Get your rifle and nail him,” Rudy said as he braked the car.

“No, you take him,” I answered. Neither of us made a move, and the buck walked slowly out of sight. While we wouldn’t admit it, both Rudy and I weren’t the least bit interested in shooting that buck.

We drove to the farmhouse, and Ross had news.

“That bunch of deer are traveling new runways,” he said. “The best one is about a mile down the road by a cornfield where. . . .”

“That’s where we just saw a buck,” I interrupted. “There’s a bunch of cedars across the road.”

“That’s the place,” Ross said. “I’d forget your other plans and pick a couple of stands along that runway.”

That’s exactly what we did. Half an hour later, I found the big sycamore I mentioned in the beginning. Rudy decided to follow the runway toward some heavily wooded ridges half a mile away.

The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

About 8 o’clock, it started raining hard. By 8:30 I was so wet I went back to the car, changed clothes, and put on a yellow rainsuit. I was almost back to the sycamore when I heard shots from Rudy’s area. I walked up on a ridge and found Rudy all excited.

“I shot at a buck with a brushpile rack,” he said. “I was curled up under a tree trying to stay dry when I heard a deer coming down the runway behind me. I turned around and we spotted each other at the same time. The buck bolted, and I cut loose with three shots. I lost his tracks right here. He sure was a big one!”

Rudy was a mighty disappointed deer hunter. He’s 35 and one of the best outdoorsmen I know. He’s been a hunting nut all his life, and he taught me how to hunt and fish when I was a boy. He lives in Mayfield where he works as a heavy-equipment operator. He’s married and has two teenage sons.

Rudy went back to his stand, and I stillhunted till noon. We met at the car for lunch, stillhunted another hour, then returned to our stands. It wasn’t long after that when I glanced over my shoulder and saw Big Red.

I don’t remember any trace of buck fever, but I do recall coldly analyzing the situation. I studied every bit of cover between myself and the deer. About 40 yards from my tree stand, a clump of cedars edged the runway. Big Red would have to pass behind that clump. When he did, I’d turn around.

My change in position came off like clockwork. When the animal appeared again he was unsuspicious, and I was in perfect shooting position with my scope lined up on his chest. I decided against squeezing the trigger. I wanted him to come as close as possible.

At the creek 30 yards away, the trophy buck stopped for a drink. The suspense was terrible. I used this moment of his relaxed alertness to suck in a deep breath. The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

Suddenly he stopped, turned his head toward his backtrack, tilted his nose, and tested the air. Then he swung his massive antlers forward and walked behind a couple of cedars where he stopped dead still. I had a feeling he was getting nervous.

He might bolt at any second, I thought. As soon as he steps from behind those cedars, I’m going to shoot.

The range was now 25 yards, and there was no question about his increased caution. His face peeked from behind the cedars. Then that unbelievable rack. Again he stood motionless. Suddenly he broke into a fast trot.

The crosswires settled at the base of his neck, and my rifle roared.

Big Red staggered sideways, regained control of his feet, and lunged straight ahead. I aimed my second shot for his shoulder, and the 240-grain bullet spun him around. He dived into thickets alongside the runway and was gone. I heard him crash through brush; then all was silent. I knew he had fallen.

I went down that tree as fast as I could. I got within 30 yards of him, and then he staggered away. I snapped two shots through the thickets, but the bullets never got to him. I heard him fall again about 60 yards to my right. I got within 40 feet of him before he tried getting up. He couldn’t make it. Another bullet finished him instantly.

I started field-dressing the buck immediately. It wasn’t easy. His bulk was so great I couldn’t move him. I tied his legs to saplings to spread-eagle his hindquarters. Throughout the job, I whistled for Rudy every few minutes. It’s a whistle note we’ve used for woods communication since we were kids. I was nearly done with the chore when Rudy found me. He stayed with the buck while I went to Ross Laster’s farm for help.

Four of the Laster brothers and I got a tractor to within 300 yards of Big Red. Then we had to chop down saplings, clear brush, and cut a fence to get the tractor within 100 yards of the buck. After that it was pure bull work — dragging, hauling, and lifting Big Red till we finally had him balanced on the tractor.

A few hours later, he weighed 260 pounds on a coal scale. I was surprised because I’d figured he would scale over 300 pounds. I guess the massive antlers fooled me. I was familiar with the Boone and Crockett Club method of scoring trophy deer, and I was certain my buck would score near the top of the record list.

Two months later, the antlers scored 185 4/8 points. My trophy won third place for typical whitetails in the Boone and Crockett Club two-year competition period ending December 31, 1965. Though I didn’t kill a new world record, I did score some impressive ratings. Big Red is the best trophy whitetail ever killed in Kentucky.

The inside spread of his rack measures 30 2/8 inches, more than 10 inches wider than the current world record. While checking the last listing of all-time Boone and Crockett records, I discovered that this inside measurement is the greatest among all typical whitetail deer recorded there. Though I realize that total score is all that counts, I doubt whether anyone will ever kill a whitetail buck with a wider antler spread than Big Red’s.

Read Next: A Son Finally Tracked Down His Dad’s Long-Lost Buck. It’s the Biggest Typical Whitetail Ever Killed in Kansas

There’s one thing I can guarantee — nobody will ever know a greater hunting thrill than I experienced when I looked over my shoulder in that sycamore and saw the dream of a lifetime coming true.

By Raymond E. Miller, as told to Jim Hayes

#8231. The World’s Most Cinematic Trail Running Is Hidden Above the Arctic Circle

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

Hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

On my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

The Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!)

Combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

Although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

The vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

While there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

Lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

It’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

Weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

Getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

Traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s important to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

Designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.

If you wear glasses, you know that finding the right ski goggles can be a little more complicated than simply picking a pair that looks good. Too-tight frames, uncomfortable pressure on your temples or the bridge of your nose, and fogged-up lenses can turn a great day on the mountain into a frustrating one. Fortunately, over-the-glasses (OTG) goggles are designed to make skiing with prescription eyewear a whole lot easier.

But comfort and compatibility aren’t the only things that matter. You still want clear optics, good ventilation, a wide field of view, and a fit that stays comfortable bell to bell. To find the best options, we tapped SKI’s experienced gear testers, who evaluated goggles across a range of conditions and skiing environments. These four stood out for their combination of comfort, performance, and value, whether you’re looking for a premium pair, a budget-friendly option, or something in between.

For glasses-wearing skiers who don’t want to spend a fortune on a dedicated OTG goggle, the Dragon DX3 L is a comfortable, no-fuss option. Its roomy frame accommodates prescription eyewear, while hypoallergenic Polartec microfleece face foam feels soft against the skin and creates a comfortable fit for all-day wear. Dragon’s cylindrical lens delivers solid peripheral vision, and its Lumalens technology enhances contrast and definition across changing light conditions. Testers put the Niseko through its paces everywhere from storm days in the Tetons to spring skiing in the Swiss Alps, praising its crisp optics and generous field of view. The MagStorm magnetic lens system also made swapping lenses easy to do on the go. #8226. The Best Trail Running Shoes for Fall 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The best trail running shoes boost our confidence on singletrack to scree fields, sand to slick rock. They’re comfortable and nimble and help us run fast or forever, depending on the adventure. As the days grow shorter and colder we’re also looking for shoes that excel under a wide variety of circumstances, like wet leaves, rime ice, and snow. And as the weather deteriorates, we’re also leaning more on road-to-trail models for the days when the roads and paths are calling our names.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across Santa Barbara to Boulder and Nebraska to New Hampshire, our testers Lisa Jhung, Cory Smith, Johnathan Beverly, and Abby Levene provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, speed, traction, cushioning, and their joy of running. The result is Trail Runner Magazine’s best trail shoes for fall 2026. Considering that the “best” shoe can run differently on someone else’s feet, our review is specially curated with a shoe claiming the title of each chosen category it achieves best. For even more models, check out Outside’s guide to best trail running shoes for fall.

Weight: 7.5 ounces (men’s 8.5), 6.2 ounces (women’s 8) Stack Height: 28.5–21.5 mm Drop: 7 mm Sizing: 7-12.5, 13, 14, 15 (men’s), 6-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Responsive and springy + Weightless feeling underfoot + Good ground feel + Excellent traction – Runs small (go half a size up) –Expensive

If the Norda 005 was a car, it would be the Mercedes AMG E63S Wagon. That is to say: it’s quiet performance luxury. IYKYK, as the kids say. Coming in at just 214 grams (7.5 ounces) for a men’s U.S. 8.5, it’s one of the lightest trail running shoes on the market. It’s also made from the highest quality materials: A Biodyneema upper makes it both durable and highly breathable. A slick of Vibram “Megagrip Elite” rubber renders the outsole ultra tacky on the trails while rolling over the roads. And, perhaps most importantly, the midsole is made completely from a proprietary Mouse Arnitel TPEE—a supercritical foam generally only used in small amounts because of the cost—making the shoe featherlight, energetic, and highly durable.

And the simplicity of the design lets the quality shine. As such, it’s a light, fast trail running shoe that can do it all. We’d turn to this shoe for anything from easy days on mixed surfaces, to “fast” trail 100-milers like Western States or Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc. Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene wore one pair of the Norda 005 for the Tour du Mont Blanc, a five-day, 110-mile adventure through the Alps, and she didn’t think about her feet once. There is no higher praise.

The midsole is tuned to be slightly firmer than the superfoam in road racers and thus provides an energetic, bouncy ride that doesn’t trampoline you in wild directions off the trail. While the lack of a plate may disqualify the Norda 005 from being a true trail “super shoe,” don’t mistake semantics for inferiority. We didn’t miss a carbon plate here, and its absence allows for enhanced ground feel and adaptability to varied terrain. The foam and rocker deliver a smooth roll and plenty of precision.

The only real downside to this shoe is the price tag. But sometimes, you get what you pay for. Read our full review of the Norda 005.

Weight: 9.5 oz (men’s), 8.4 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 32–28 mm Drop: 4 mm Sizing: 7-13, 14, 15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Lightweight and nimble – Slippery laces require double-knotting

We’ve tested every version of the Saucony Peregrine since the model’s debut in 2011, and this sixteenth iteration just might be our all-time favorite. The shoe has long been capable of making us feel nimble on rugged terrain, with its great balance of ground feel and cushioning, plus traction on all kinds of trail, wrapped up in a lightweight package. But version 16 takes the Peregrine’s trail capabilities to new levels, and at $150, it’s an easy pick for Best Value.

The upgraded Vibram Megagrip outsole grips rock slabs with aplomb, while the four-millimeter lugs dig into loose dirt and soft ground (though some sandy-trail testers craved even deeper, toothier lugs). The balanced midsole—not too springy, not too mushy, not too thick—delivers a strong connection to the trail while still feeling responsive and shock absorbing, even during wild descents. The flexible, breathable mesh upper with added toe protection kept out trail debris and warded off snags from roots and branches.

The fit of this trail running shoe somehow made a variety of testers feel like it was custom-made for them. It locks down the heel, and the just-roomy-enough toebox allowed toe space to breathe while maintaining control. “The fit is just perfect,” said a tester. “I feel secure and supported from heel to toe, and side to side.”

Weight: 10 oz (men’s), 9 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 33.5 mm–25.5 mm Drop: 8mm Sizing: 7-13, 14 (men’s), 5-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Great traction + Outstanding foothold – Cushioning may feel too firm for some

The Salomon Genesis 2 earned mountain-goat status among our crew, providing outstanding traction over loose dirt and rock. Its supportive Matryx upper—constructed with thin, high-tenacity yarns and durable Kevlar—secures narrow and wide feet alike via Salomon’s quick-pull lacing system. The forefoot offers slightly more room than version 1, enhancing overall comfort without sacrificing agility.

The outsole, made of Salomon’s Contagrip rubber with toothy, 4 mm lugs, provided excellent traction on all surfaces, giving us confidence, even on scrambles over large rocky slabs and slippery descents.

While the EVA-blend midsole runs firm, it offers direct trail feedback. “This shoe makes it fun to pick a line and charge,” noted one tester. “I felt completely present instead of mindlessly rolling over obstacles.”

For technical runners who prefer softer cushioning, we also recommend the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro. (Read our full review of the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro here.)

The Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the new model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

The midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

What makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. This shoe’s versatility makes it a great pick as a one-trick pony for the casual runner who doesn’t need a lighter, faster race shoe, and a solid choice for travel.

Weight: 9.5 oz (unisex) Stack Height: 40–34 mm Drop: 6 mm Sizing: 5-12,13 (men’s), 6.5-13.5, 14.5 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag

Brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has launched in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

If you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

When assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

Ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

If the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how quickly and powerfully it rebounds.

The best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, quickly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research shows that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate new releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall update, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to New Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

Freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and says her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

His obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

Jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and quickly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every new model as they were released.
