#8119. 8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

You’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

A little online searching will quickly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

Tired of the practically impossible task of packing up the family for a holiday? Here are the best packing cubes for busy families on the go.

For many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

When it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

Along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to plan. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

Unleash your little one's love for Lightning McQueen with these top-rated Cars playsets and figures.

As tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:

Of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a big decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

What are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Weather is a big factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

The umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even said the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only issue they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!)

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

When you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

The charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

The Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or shows, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

The stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Traveling with kids doesn't;t have to mean getting rid of your entire beauty routine.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

These wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

My family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

They come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

The fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

To pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

The stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Could your child use a little encouragement to read? Disney is here to help with these fabulous books for kids ages 5 to 9.

Take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

#8118. How To Get Fantastic Sleep

Are parents doomed to a lifetime of chasing after good sleep?

On a tip from a savvy movie critic, I took my 7-year-old out to see his second ever Marvel movie the other day (he's a big fan of Norse mythology so he's seen Thor: Ragnarok and sorta liked it). We sat back, donning our 3D glasses (he was very into the novelty of this) and took in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. What a pleasant surprise. The movie is, in fact, as my movie critic colleague promised, The Best Marvel Movie for Families.

For the kids, there’s a lot to love. There are the action montages, a bright retro futuristic setting, a visual style that is gee-whiz superhero cool, but in a comic way — shiny and light and not over the top. The movie is just more palatable for kids than most other Marvel movies, emotionally and cognitively. The superheroes are relatable as family but they also play the part of role models well, interacting with and caring deeply about the public they serve. The villain, too, is not so much motivated by evil but by an unstoppable appetite (for planets, granted) that he is actively trying to rid himself of. A little sympathy goes a long way to take the teeth out of a monster. But most importantly there’s Franklin, the baby.

The Fantastic Four are a family and have arguments and issues that are familiar to all kids. One big one is the strain (and joys) that having a baby puts on, well, everyone. I especially loved seeing Reed Richards and Sue Storm, superheroes with doctorates who no doubt have seen their share of sleep debt, complain about tiredness. Even genius superheroes can’t face the superheroic task that is getting baby to bed. It’s a tension that gets the screen time it deserves. Just ask any parent.

Sleep has been on my mind a lot lately. I always thought that I would crush sleep once my baby grew up, but some 6 years later I realize maybe it wasn’t the baby? I’ve never met someone who doesn’t have a tenuous relationship with sleep. When I was in physical prime either during my senior high school years as a soccer player and middle distant runner or during my marathon-happy thirties, I slept so very soundly. At least that’s how I remember it.

Now that I’m older I juggle more — so much more — work out a little less and do a lot more staring at the ceiling in the middle of the night. With age, I maybe need to admit, I need an assist.

I’ve only just started to give sleep tracking a fair shake. I’ve been pairing up a new Samsung Galaxy 8 watch with a Samsung Galaxy Ring (I’ve been a Samsung man since I converted to their Flip phone, which pairs seamlessly together, requiring no third-party apps).

So what have I found? That data is in fact motivating. I won’t get too into the weeds but I will tell you that late night snacks, screens, night caps, and work are bad for my sleep. Evening walks, reading, and days with lighter fare and more quality workouts lead to more quality sleep.

It’s all fairly obvious stuff, but what the tracking does is force the attention. Good sleep matters and is, for those of us without babies, a fairly controllable thing. We can create habits that help sleep. We can choose to prioritize our health and well being. Stats don’t tell us what to do, but they do show what our current priorities.

When my son was a sleepless baby (he really was the worst) the only two priorities I had were to keep him healthy (alive) and to find sleep. My world is a little easier now and my list of priorities has grown immensely. I want to be outdoors more, to find new fitness, to take on new passions (birding is kind of fun, everyone), to embrace a new phase of marriage, to learn new skills, and meet my kids where they are. But sometimes you have to remember the basics. Without good sleep, everything is more difficult. Only a superhero can defeat the eater of worlds on a new parent’s sleep schedule. The rest of us need all the help we can get.

#8115. Hunger Games Fans, Did You Spot These 12 Hidden Plant Meanings in Sunrise on the Reaping?

Hidden in plain sight in the posters and trailers, these 12 plants could reveal more than you think about The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's something about Suzanne Collins' iconic dystopian series that feels more relevant than ever, and, with the latest film taking us back to the 50th Hunger Games, there's plenty for fans to scrutinize beyond the action itself. Personally, though, I can't stop looking at the plants.

If you've followed the franchise, you'll know that nature has never been merely decorative in Panem. From sinister plants and poisonous berries to the natural world providing food, healing plants, and shelter, knowing your botany in the arena can quite literally mean the difference between life and death.

There's also a long literary tradition of using plants as an act of resistance. After all, flowers have carried hidden messages for centuries, from the symbolism of roses in mythology to the elaborate Victorian language of flowers, when a carefully chosen bouquet could communicate everything from secret affection to heartbreak.

Watch The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Trailer:

A post shared by The Hunger Games (@thehungergames)

Even the names of some of the franchise's most memorable characters have botanical connections. Katniss is named after Sagittaria latifolia, a real North American aquatic plant also known as a swamp potato thanks to its edible tubers – making it a rather fitting namesake for a character whose survival instincts are so closely connected to the natural world.

Rue, meanwhile, shares her name with an aromatic herb traditionally associated with regret and sorrow (which is heartbreaking when you consider her story). And it seems the trailers and posters for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping suggest that the franchise's botanical language is far from finished.

From wildflowers carpeting the arena to carefully arranged floral displays around some of Panem's most recognisable characters, there are plenty of plants worth looking twice at in the posters and trailers alike.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Some have fascinating historical meanings, others have surprisingly sinister botanical properties, and more than a few might offer clues about the story's characters and themes.

With that in mind, then, here are 12 botanical details I've spotted – and what they could mean.

The striking urn plant, Aechmea fasciata, is a popular bromeliad that's hard to miss in the above Sunrise On The Reaping poster thanks to its architectural rosette of silvery-green leaves and bright pink flower spike.

Its name comes from the distinctive cup formed by its overlapping leaves, which collects water in its natural habitat. This adaptation helps the plant make the most of the resources around it, even when growing conditions are challenging.

It's easy to see why it makes an interesting symbol in the Hunger Games universe. Urn plants are associated with resilience, adaptation and protection – qualities that are essential when survival is the ultimate prize. There's something particularly fitting about a plant that creates its own little reservoir of resources in a world where nothing comes easily, right?

Foxgloves (Digitalis purpurea) are among Britain's most recognisable wildflowers. Their tall flower spikes and bell-shaped blooms make them a favourite with pollinators and cottage garden enthusiasts... but there's a darker side to these pretty flowers. Every part of the foxglove plant is poisonous, containing compounds called cardiac glycosides that affect the heart.

Interestingly, those same compounds have played an important role in medicine. Digitalis-derived drugs have been used to treat certain heart conditions, making foxgloves a fascinating example of how the line between medicine and poison can depend on the dose.

In the Hunger Games, then, foxgloves could represent the duality of healing and danger – something that feels particularly at home in an arena where even the most beautiful things can be deadly.

White roses have long been associated with innocence, purity and remembrance. In Victorian flower dictionaries, their meanings included innocence, silence and even a holy death. Their appearance around President Snow is therefore particularly interesting, especially considering he's one of Panem's most ruthless figures.

Could they be a visual reminder of the innocence destroyed by the Capitol? Or perhaps a suggestion that even the most pristine-looking things can conceal something rotten underneath?

If white roses suggest purity, red roses are traditionally associated with passionate love and desire. They have been used for centuries as declarations of affection, but their symbolism isn't always straightforward. In the Victorian language of flowers, different shades and arrangements could carry different messages, from deep devotion to longing.

When red roses appear around President Snow, it's difficult not to consider the contrast between romantic passion and the bloodshed associated with his regime. After all, their vivid color also makes them an interesting counterpart to the white roses. Together, then, the two colors create a visual language of innocence, passion, power and mortality... which is very Hunger Games-coded.

The California poppy (Eschscholzia californica) is instantly recognisable by its bright orange flowers. Native to western North America, it's also the official state flower of California. It's a hardy plant that thrives in sunny conditions and can tolerate relatively poor soils, making it a lovely symbol of resilience.

Poppies have different meanings across cultures, but they're frequently associated with remembrance, sleep and renewal. The California poppy's connection to the American landscape, though, makes it particularly interesting in the world of the Hunger Games, especially as it reimagines a future North America as Panem... especially as its bright and cheerful appearance feels so ironic against the darker world in which the Games take place.

Try the Burpee Sunset Mixed California Poppy Flower Seed from Walmart if you're in the mood for shades of orange, yellow, and cream in your own garden. You can even sow the seeds directly into gravel or cracks, too!

If you've spotted the sunflowers in the character poster for Percy Daggs IV as Ampert, you're not alone in wondering what they mean for the new Hunger Games film. After all, it's difficult to look at a sunflower (Helianthus annuus) without thinking of sunshine, happiness and optimism.

These towering annuals are often associated with hope, loyalty and resilience. Their ability to grow quickly and produce impressive flower heads makes them a familiar symbol of strength and positivity, and there's also a lovely modern interpretation of sunflower symbolism that centers on community and supporting one another through difficult times.

In a story where alliances can mean survival? Well, that sense of solidarity feels particularly poignant.

Canterbury bells (Campanula medium) are charming cottage garden flowers with tall stems covered in nodding bell-shaped blooms. And, fun fact, they're also the birth month biennial for May babies, too!

Their traditional Victorian flower meaning was 'acknowledgement', while other historical dictionaries associated them more generally with constancy. And, in a story about loyalty, friendship and the people we stand alongside when times get difficult, both interpretations feel rather fitting.

Celebrate the Tributes' attempt to break the machine, then, with a packet of Canterbury Bells Double Mix from Amazon.

The unusual pincushion protea, from the genus Leucospermum, has an unmistakable appearance. Its spiky flower heads look almost like elaborate fireworks or, as the name suggests, a pincushion.

Native to southern Africa, these evergreen shrubs are adapted to challenging growing conditions and are known for their striking flowers. Proteas more broadly, though, have become associated with transformation, strength, courage and diversity. As such, their unusual appearance also makes them a natural symbol of individuality.

Their presence around Effie Trinket is a possible nod to her flamboyant personality, as Effie has always been someone who embraces color, extravagance and standing out from the crowd, even when the world around her is anything but cheerful. Peersonally, though, this writer thinks it might be a nod to her eventual character arc...

Toadstools might not technically be plants – they're fungi, as we made very clear in our recent piece on birth month mushrooms – but they deserve a place in this botanical spotter's guide.

Fungi are essential to healthy ecosystems, breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil. Some species, however, are highly poisonous, while others have medicinal or mind-altering properties, and that contrast gives mushrooms a fascinating symbolic role. They can represent decay and death, but also renewal, transformation and altered states of consciousness.

In the world of the Hunger Games, where the natural environment is often manipulated to confuse, frighten or kill its inhabitants? I suspect toadstools are a fitting reminder that not everything growing in the wild should be trusted.

Bee balm (Monarda) is a North American perennial loved by bees, butterflies and hummingbirds. Its colorful and nectar-rich flowers (particularly this stunning Pocahontas Purple Rose Bee Balm from Nature Hills) make it a wonderful addition to pollinator-friendly gardens, while the plant also has a history of traditional herbal use.

Today, bee balm is sometimes associated with compassion, empathy and comfort during difficult times. An RHS study of historical flower dictionaries, however, reveals that one nineteenth-century interpretation of this super-spreader was rather less affectionate: "Your whims are quite unbearable".

That's quite a contrast to the modern associations of care and kindness – and makes its appearance in the sinister world of the Hunger Games all the more intriguing... especially for those who remember the role they played in the Sunrise On The Reaping book.

Now here's a botanical detail I particularly love, as Nepenthes is a genus of tropical carnivorous plants, commonly known as tropical pitcher plants. Their distinctive modified leaves form hanging pitchers filled with digestive fluid, which trap and break down insects and other small prey.

The genus name has a fascinating origin. It comes from the Greek word nepenthes, associated with a mythical substance that banished sorrow or grief, which is an extraordinary name for a plant that catches and digests its victims.

In the context of the Hunger Games, the contrast is almost too good to ignore. A plant whose name evokes freedom from grief, but whose survival strategy involves trapping and consuming other creatures? Surely that's a dark metaphor for Panem itself (and almost worth buying a purple pitcher plant from the Ragnaroc Storein the run-up to the film, too).

A post shared by The Hunger Games (@thehungergames)

Spanish bluebells (Hyacinthoides hispanica) are popular spring-flowering bulbs, producing upright stems covered in clusters of blue, pink or white bell-shaped flowers. Unlike native blooms, though, these can spread vigorously in gardens and hybridize with native bluebells – something which hhis has raised concerns about the genetic integrity of native woodland populations.

The resulting hybrids can be difficult to identify, and experts advise gardeners living close to native bluebell populations to avoid planting Spanish bluebells. In terms of the Hunger Games, then, it's an interesting possible metaphor for displacement, hybridization and the arrival of an outsider that changes an established ecosystem.

In a story so concerned with power, territory and the destruction of existing communities, it feels like an idea well worth considering.

Beyond the individual plants seen across the posters and trailers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, it's the wider meadow-like landscape of the arena that deserves attention.

Wildflowers are usually associated with freedom, biodiversity and the natural world growing without human interference, and tend to evoke a sense of peace and escape from the pressures of modern life. This arena, though, turns that idea on its head, forcing nature to become a part of the spectacle. Its beauty is carefully presented, but the environment is ultimately controlled by the Gamemakers. A field of flowers might look like an idyllic meadow, yet it exists within a space designed to test, manipulate and endanger the tributes.

It's a clever contrast between the natural world as something beautiful and life-giving, and nature as something that can be manipulated into a weapon. And perhaps that's the biggest botanical message of all: in Panem, you should never assume that anything is harmless. Even something as simple and innocuous as, say, a flower.

#8114. The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

How should we all tackle phone use and screen time? An ancient Eleusinian mystery may hold the answer.

Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?

I don’t see much evidence of it out there. Personally, the phone is undeniably useful but still feels like a foreign object in my hand — a feeling that was brought into stark relief the second my kids were old enough to pick up a screen. To them, a tablet or phone offers an enticing, comforting, and even productive space. Not healthy, exactly, but familiar. For me, it’s alien — and ground zero for a cultural battle against brain rot, attention loss, and reality itself. Phones stress me out.

I ran into a much needed perspective on this dilemma in a long, thoughtful essay by Karl Ove Knausgaard, the brilliant Norwegian writer with an uncanny ability to see the world as it is, in meticulous detail. My struggle, as he helped me to see, comes from those most influential years in my life — the years before the smartphone. “To understand a man, you have to know what was happening in the world when he was twenty, Napoleon is supposed to have said,” writes Knausgaard in Harper’s Magazine. “The quotation is probably apocryphal, but that doesn’t mean it’s not true.”

My Napoleonic prime was in the 2000s — shortly after the advent of Facebook, but right before the iPhone was in everyone’s hands. For Knausgaard, who is 56 years old, the internet barely existed in his twenties. He admits that he has been ignoring the fundamental influences of such technological advances since. “Not once in those forty years have I turned my attention to technology and tried to understand it,” Knausgaard writes, “how it works in itself, how it works in me. It’s as if I had moved to a foreign country and not bothered to learn its language, as if I am content with not understanding what is happening around me and just settling for my own little world. This lately feels like serious neglect.”

This resonates. While I spend considerable time trying to understand and control the impacts of screen time on my kids' developing brains, I hardly pay attention to my own use. What am I doing when I check for emails, Slack messages, and texts with lab rat-like repetition, or scroll Reddit News and The New York Times at every down moment, or get lost in Instagram and YouTube rabbit holes? More importantly, what should I do about it?

Knausgaard found his technological insight by heading out to Athens, Greece to talk to James Bridle, an author and artist with a specialty in nonhuman ways of thinking (and what orangutans can teach us about politics). In a sense, Bridle sees technology as getting in the way of experience. Sounding like a free range parenting proselytizer, he says that “the only thing you can do is experience it and do it yourself. You have to do it, you have to experience it, it has to happen to you. Bodily, physically — because you’re part of the world.”

Bridle takes this deeper, offering the example of an ancient Eleusinian cult in which initiates were led into a dark room, shown a “whirlwind of impressions, without anyone telling them what they were seeing or what it meant” and being left to interpret that on their own. The next year, they were shown the initiation from the outside, “and you could say that only then, when the gaze from within was complemented by the gaze from without, was the initiation completed.”

This metaphor for the digital world made it all click for me. We’re all too often inside looking at the whirlwind of the internet with little control and understanding. There are more of us now trying to step outside of this world — to see the puppet masters at play in order to walk away from it all.

We’re not going back to 2006, that innocent year before the iPhone was introduced. And I don’t think that should be the goal. The technology that has been introduced since my childhood is incredible, powerful, and a big piece of human progress. But it’s no replacement for the real world lessons I get when I put down the phone and experience life, unfiltered.

#8112. The Resentment of Being the Parent Who Can Never Clock Out

Maybe it’s a lack of freedom, unequal responsibilities with a partner, or both, but you’re big mad.

You had a certain expectation for what new motherhood would look like: Friends and family stopping by, your partner playing peek-a-boo with the baby, and even yourself feeling calm, patient, and present when the baby cries.

Reality might look a bit different, though. You blink, and your partner heads back to work, reading a newly cracked novel on the commute. Your friend drops by with pastries, then jets off to a yoga class. Everyone’s gone but you and the baby.

You’re at home, wading through a pile of burp cloths and hoping the baby naps long enough for you to choke down a sandwich. If you’re feeling a little ragey about that, you’re not alone. In one 2022 cross-sectional survey, nearly a third of new moms reported feeling intense anger.

But who are you actually angry with, and are you even mad, or — let's be brutally honest for a second — just jealous of their freedom and spontaneity? What’s really going on is likely more complicated than that, but there are things you can do things about it besides screaming into a pillow.

Anger is often underrepresented in research on the postpartum period, and tends to fly under the radar when moms get screened for perinatal depressive and anxiety disorders, as it can occur without elevated depressive symptoms, says Christine Ou, Ph.D., lead author of the aforementioned survey, assistant professor at the University of Victoria in Canada, and founder of the school’s Parent-Child Lab. “So asking only about depression may miss mothers who are struggling [with anger],” she says.

In a 2018 review, which Ou co-authored, researchers found that several factors contributed to moms’ anger, including a feeling of powerlessness and a misalignment between expectations and reality.

But you can also feel angry simply because having a newborn is hard. Moms were often mad because “their needs were compromised, and they were exhausted or stressed,” says Ou, as to why many new moms reported feeling anger. That’s pretty par for the course during the newborn haze, but being stuck at home — especially without help or breaks — can intensify those emotions.

Babies can bring a lot of joy, but staying at home around the clock with one is no picnic. First, newborns operate on an unpredictable schedule and demand constant supervision, making it feel like a logistical nightmare to get out of the house. Compounding that, mothers have historically been cast as the ‘default parent,’ says Paige Bellenbaum, L.C.S.W., the director of strategy and impact at Columbia University’s Center for the Transition to Parenthood. In traditional families, they’re “the ones physically with the baby most of the day and night, carrying most of the mental and emotional load, and managing the logistics, often while preparing for their own return to work,” says Bellenbaum.

Even if parents split duties pretty evenly within their own orbit, external factors can still throw that balance off. Take the fragmented, inadequate, and deeply unequal parental leave in the US: Often the dad or non-birthing partner ends up returning to work first. When that happens, the parent who remains at home “may feel envy, anger, or a sense of abandonment,” says Bellenbaum. Being home day in and day out with a baby can be isolating, even if you do get help from family or well-meaning visitors, she adds.

It's not just one person returning to work that creates this isolation. Reliable childcare can cost as much as your monthly mortgage these days, which means many birthing parents may make the tough but economical decision to stay home with the baby. “Everyone else can come and go, while she remains responsible for the baby, with no real opportunity to step away,” says Ou.

You could argue that the parent who’s heading into the office doesn’t necessarily want to be away from their family nor view it as an “escape.” Nevertheless, they “get to step back into their former life, stopping for coffee on the way into work, using the bathroom when they need to, and feeling useful and connected to the outside world,” says Bellenbaum. Plus, heading back to work can restore elements of their pre-baby life they may have been missing, like adult conversation, structure, control, and a sense of mastery and accomplishment, she adds. Meanwhile, the mom at home takes a 30-second shower and sings Wheels on the Bus for the 40th time in a row.

It’s normal to feel a lot of emotions in the postpartum phase — joy, frustration, rage, loneliness, anxiety, sadness, gratitude, you name it, says Ou. But that mix can make it hard to figure out exactly what you’re feeling.

While postpartum anger can happen independent of PPD, the two are clearly linked. For instance, Ou’s survey found that anger and PPD can also occur at the same time; in fact, those who screened positive for depressive symptoms had almost four times the odds of reporting intense anger. (But the survey couldn’t establish which came first.)

It’s not surprising: Imagine telling people you’re feeling trapped in your house — and no one seems to care. “When the circumstances behind a mother’s anger don’t change, when she remains overwhelmed, unsupported, or unheard, she may start to feel helpless or hopeless, which could contribute to depression,” says Ou. Maybe your partner acknowledges the struggle but doesn’t actually change anything, or you don’t feel comfortable or safe expressing your anger. Both can contribute to the development of PPD.

You might feel guilty for feeling trapped in the first place. After all, aren’t moms supposed to want to soak up as much time as possible with their babies? And, in a country where parental leave isn’t guaranteed, isn’t it a privilege to be at home with your newborn? Despite these arguments being flawed — they’re ignorant of the realities of newborn needs and nonexistent help for moms — this narrative can put a lot of pressure on moms, or even make you feel like you’re not doing right by your child. “Guilt and shame about being angry can add to that distress, potentially contributing to or worsening depressive symptoms,” says Ou.

First, know that it’s normal to be angry or irritable—period. But if you notice yourself getting worked up, take stock of how often you get angry, and how mad you get. If anger is frequent, intense, difficult to manage, or affecting your relationships or everyday life, that warrants a discussion with your doctor, says Ou. As is “feeling scared by your anger, or that you have little control over your reactions,” she adds. Postpartum Support International offers a peer support group for postpartum anger and rage, which may be a potential resource.

A screening from your healthcare provider can also be helpful since it may factor in other symptoms like crying and sadness, changes in sleep or appetite, a lack of interest in the baby, a sense of hopelessness or helplessness, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, according to Bellenbaum. “When these are present along with the anger, PPD may be at play,” she says.

However, getting professional help is not a replacement for making changes in your home and routine, if needed, stresses Bellenbaum. These tactics can help.

Since anger often stems from a lack of equality, it helps to start by looking at the division of labor in a partnered relationship. “Who gets more opportunities to sleep?” says Ou. “Who can leave without making arrangements? Who notices what needs doing, and who is responsible for making sure it happens?” Assessing this together allows you both to see who’s shouldering more of the work. “When that load is shared more equitably, resentment tends to ease, and a sense of shared responsibility emerges,” says Bellenbaum.

If and when you identify the areas of inequality, the partner should take “more ownership of tasks, night shifts, and the mental planning, not just ‘helping’,” says Bellenbaum, who recommends a card-based system called Fair Play that helps partners rebalance household work and divide invisible mental labor (like remembering to schedule doctor appointments). “Instead of splitting every chore 50/50, each partner takes full ownership of specific responsibilities, divided in a way that both people feel is fair,” she says.

“Genuine off-duty time means someone else is fully responsible for the baby,” says Bellenbaum. In other words, mom’s not on standby. She’s not listening for cries or manning the monitor, and she’s also not checking her phone or expecting a call because her partner feels the baby “wants mommy,” she explains. That can be hard, especially if the mom is afraid to leave the baby or feels guilty about being away, but it’s a worthwhile exercise for everyone. Otherwise, it “can make it harder for her partner to learn to care for the baby on their own,” she says.

Non-partnered parents need breaks, too. “Friends and family can bring food, do laundry, or hold the baby for half an hour,” says Ou. Run errands alone one evening while the baby stays home with a loved one. “A grocery run might be a chore, but it can also mean getting out of the house, being alone, and deciding what happens next without having to respond to a baby and their needs,” she says.

If a new mom in your life is dealing with anger or isolation, there are ways you can support her. Instead of asking what she needs, be specific and offer choices, like "I can do some laundry for you or bring over food for you. Which would help more?” says Bellenbaum.

If going out with friends or on a date night feels like too much for the mom, that's okay. "Separating from the baby is hard, and it often takes small steps before big ones,” says Bellenbaum. In this case, offer to watch the baby while she goes for a walk, go grocery shopping with her while you push the stroller, or hold the baby at the salon while she gets a haircut.

The bottom line? Feeling angry because your world feels small right now doesn’t make you a bad mom. “You can love your baby and resent having so little freedom over your own time,” says Ou. “Both things can be true.” It just means you need more sleep, a conversation with other adults, or an hour or two out of the house, and having those needs met only makes you a better parent to your baby.

Those tiny black flies are only part of the story. A raw potato slice on the soil can reveal what's underneath for next to nothing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You water your houseplant, and a little cloud of tiny black flies lifts off the soil. A minute later, they're on the window. Fungus gnats turn up in many homes once fall arrives, and they can hang around all winter. The next batch is already growing in the pot, and a fungus gnat potato trap is an easy way to find them.

Before you read up on how to get rid of fungus gnats, take a look at what's going on in the pot. The adult flies you keep swatting don't feed on your plants, but their larvae are a different story. Those live in the damp potting mix just under the surface, out of sight unless you go digging.

One raw potato saves you the digging. Lay a slice on the soil, and the larvae come up to feed on it. Lift it a couple of days later, and whatever is in the pot is often feeding on the underside. Odds are there's a potato in the pantry already, so finding out costs you pretty much nothing, really.

A fungus gnat's whole life happens in or around the pot. They're small flies, often in the genus Bradysia, and a female can lay up to 200 eggs in damp potting mix. Once they hatch, the larvae eat for a couple of weeks and pupate near the surface, and new adults show up a week or so later. At room temperature, that's roughly three to four weeks per generation – so a few flies in October can be a lot more by the holidays.

It's the larvae doing the eating. Their usual food is fungi and rotting organic matter, but they'll go after fine root hairs too. While a minor infestation won't usually do any harm, enough of them can damage roots and stunt growth, especially in seedlings and young plants. Watch for something like a tiny worm: clear or whitish, no legs, a shiny black head, ¼ inch (6 mm) long at most.

Cut a raw potato into slices about ¼ inch (6.4 mm) thick. Set one cut side down on the potting mix, and press it lightly so it sits flat. That contact is the whole trick. Larvae move up to the potato as a food source and gather on the moist underside where it touches the soil.

Give it a day or two before the first look. Flip the slice and check its underside, then the soil where it sat, for tiny clear larvae. Against dark, wet potting mix, they're hard to pick out, though, so a magnifying glass, like this Rongon 10X folding pocket magnifier from Amazon, helps a lot. Nothing there yet? Set it back down for another day or two. Sometimes larvae can take a few days to find the potato.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Don't leave it there for good, though. Raw potato breaks down in damp soil, and a rotting slice is just more of the decaying material larvae feed on. Toss the old one in the trash, larvae and all, and put down a fresh slice. Used like this, potato slices for fungus gnats let you track whether the numbers are dropping. Eggs won't show up on it. They don't feed, so they stay put in the mix.

So, do potatoes kill fungus gnats? Not really. The potato doesn't poison anything – it just draws feeding larvae up from the roots, and tossing a slice with larvae on it removes those ones. Eggs, pupae, and the adults flying around the room aren't affected.

Use the potato to check on things, then reach for something else to fix it. Say the slice comes up clean. That's nice, but it doesn't mean the pot's clear. Maybe there are only a few larvae, or they weren't feeding much. If flies keep hanging around, put down another slice.

Too much water keeps a lot of fungus gnat problems going. Short days and cool rooms slow houseplants down in fall and winter, so they use less water. Water like it's still July, and the mix stays wet, which eggs and larvae love. Let the top inch (2.5cm) dry before watering again. Empty the saucer, and make sure the pot drains. Old mix holds extra water as it breaks down. If a plant's due for repotting, look for a fresh mix with perlite for drainage, like the Back to the Roots Indoor Potting Mix, available from Walmart.

Yellow sticky traps are for the adults. Push a few into the pot – you can buy sticky traps cheaply from Amazon. Each female stuck to one won't lay any more eggs, and the count tells you if things are improving. Down in the soil, the larvae aren't touched. If the gnats won't let up, try Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. israelensis), a naturally occurring soil bacterium. Despite the name, it isn't the Bt sprayed on caterpillars. This strain targets only fly larvae.

Summit Mosquito Bits use Bti to control both mosquito and fungus gnat larvae. Rather than scattering the granules on the soil, it's best to soak them in water for about 30 minutes, then apply that water to your houseplant soil. Repeat application about every five days, since Bti doesn't last long indoors.

Beneficial nematodes (Steinernema feltiae), such as BioLogic's Scanmask nematodes, are another organic option. These microscopic roundworms seek out fungus gnat larvae in potting soil. They enter the larvae and release bacteria that kill them, then feed and reproduce inside their bodies. It's pretty gruesome, but effective. They arrive alive in the mail, so use them right away. Keep the soil moist and the temperature between 60 and 90°Fahrenheit (16–32°C), or they won't work. Whichever you buy, check that the label allows indoor potted plants, then follow it.

Catching larvae early makes a fungus gnat problem much easier to control. A few larvae in one pot make for a far smaller job than a houseful of flies a month from now – and a potato slice is a cheap way to see whether your houseplant soil is hiding them.

So keep a potato around this winter. Set a fresh slice down whenever the flies show up again, and go easier on the watering while days are short. Fungus gnats have a much harder time of it once the top of the soil dries out between drinks!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8110. What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and important meditation about masculinity.

Will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

“I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he said to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

When it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he says, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”

Finally, he says that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”

In 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

Danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

Masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

#8109. When can a kid ride in the front seat?

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

Has your big kid started asking – or downright begging – to graduate to the front seat of the car finally? Most kids start pining for the coveted spot long before they are big enough to safely sit up front.

Of course,safetyis your number one concern, butas their endless pleas wear you down, you might be wondering:when can I let them sit up front? Is it really that big of a deal to keep them in the back? We’ve been there. For help, we reached out to childhood safety experts to understand why the AAP recommends waiting until at least the age of 13 before letting your child ride in the front seat.

While the AAP guidelines are clear, local and federal laws (or, rather, lack thereof) muddy the waters. Lia Tuso, a Child Passenger Safety Technician (CPST) based in Buffalo, New York, tells Moms.com, “Unfortunately, when it comes to child passenger safety, the laws are the bare minimum.” There are no federal laws in the U.S. prohibiting children from riding in the front seat, but there are a handful of state laws. Delaware, for example, requires children to be at least 12 years old and 65 inches tall to sit in the front seat, while California mandates that children must be eight years old and over 57 inches tall. And it’s not just the U.S. – other peer nations’ laws are surprisingly lax around the topic. Most state laws in Australia, for example, require children to be at least seven years old to ride shotgun.

Tuso does not mince words about why younger children in the front seat of a car is so dangerous, saying, “The frontal airbags are designed to protect adult male bodies, not pre-pubescent children. The frontal airbags deploy at about 200 mph and they are designed to make contact with the average-sized male adult's bones. They simply aren't designed to protect children who don't have the same bone strength as an adult.”

While predicting your pre-teen son's future height isn't an exact science there are ways to see if he's above or below the average height of his peers

Corri Miller-Hobbs, a safety expert with the Children's Hospital of Richmond at VCU, agrees. She also oversees the Virginia chapter Safe Kids Worldwide and tells Moms.com, “[Keeping children under 13 in the back seat] places the child in a seating position that is further away from a frontal crash, the most common type of crash.”

Tuso points out that research performed by the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia shows that children who are exposed to frontal airbags are twice as likely to suffer injury than children riding in the back seat. “The injuries that are most frequently seen from children riding in the front seat are head injuries such as traumatic brain injury and superficial head trauma, thoracic/chest injuries, abdominal injuries, pelvic injuries, and orthopedic injuries such as long bone fractures,” Dr. Alexis Javier, a Pediatrician with Memorial Hermann Health System in Houston, Texas, tells Moms.com. Importantly, Miller-Hobbs adds, “Injuries vary and can depend on how close the child is sitting to the frontal airbag and whether they were correctly restrained with a child restraint or safety belt.”

Tuso recommends seeking guidance from Child Passenger Safety Technician for every car seat transition, saying that too often, “parents will schedule a car seat installation check with a CPST for their newborn, but don't finish the journey to the front seat.”

“Oftentimes we see kids sitting upfront, who should still not only be in the back seat, but also in a booster!” Tuso says, “Most children will need a booster until ten to 12 years old. So parents should first ask, has the child maxed out the height/weight limits on their current booster seat?”

In addition to being physically developed enough to be safe in the front seat, Tuso shares important guidelines to ensure the correct fit for an adult seatbelt on a child, called the Five-Step Test.

“Even if your child passes the seat belt fit test in one seating position in one vehicle, that doesn’t mean they will pass the test in all vehicles and seating positions… so be sure to perform the seat belt fit test in any vehicle and any seating position your child may utilize,” Miller-Hobbs says. She also advises moving the passenger seat as far back from the airbag as possible for your child.

“Be sure to consider your child’s developmental level and personality when explaining the rationale,” Miller-Hobbs says, “Avoid using scary details about injuries versus talking about making healthy and safe choices, as with other aspects of their life.” She offers a few ideas to help make the backseat more appealing, such as:

Adventures have never been more fun, or easy, with one of these 8 travel essentials.

Tuso adds that watching crash test videos together on YouTube can be an effective way to demonstrate the necessity for strict rules around riding up front. “There is a lot of peer pressure around this age, especially with school drop-offs, but reminding your child of the importance of riding safely will set them up for success... even when they're driving on their own!” she says.

“We understand caregivers and children are excited and proud when new milestones are achieved,” Miller-Hobbs adds, “However, moving out of a car seat or belt positioning booster seat into a seat belt system should not be a milestone that is rushed.” Tuso agrees, saying, “The safest place for children under 13 is the back seat. While growing up is inevitable, injuries are preventable... there's no rush to the front seat.”

#8108. A Change of Scenery Should Be Part of Your PPD Recovery

When the walls start closing in, a shift in your surroundings can help.

Even 13 years later, Graeme Seabrook can still vividly remember how she felt when she got home from the hospital with her newborn son.

“It was like a gray wall had come down between me and the world, and everybody else was on the other side,” she says. “I was on this side with this tiny baby who depended on me for everything. And I felt all-consuming rage, like 24/7; nothing made me happy. Nothing made me even peaceful. It was really hard to sleep. Breastfeeding was torturous. It was scary.”

Seabrook, now a mom of two, says she felt claustrophobic in her two-bedroom home in Charleston, SC, where she lived at the time.

“It felt like I didn't have any air in that house because there was baby stuff everywhere,” she says. “I had no place to go. I had no way to get out. And even when I tried to, my anxiety was so bad that I couldn't leave.”

Seabrook was ultimately diagnosed with postpartum depression (PPD) and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and, with treatment, was able to emerge from the fog. She now lives in Colorado and created Whole Human Mama, an online support space for moms.

But you don’t need a diagnosis to know what it’s like to feel trapped. It’s common for new moms to feel stuck at home, even without PPD, says Catherine Monk, Ph.D., psychologist and division chief of Women’s Mental Health in the Department of Obstetrics & Gynecology at Columbia University.

Postpartum brings on a dramatic lifestyle shift. During pregnancy, you may still be going to work, meeting friends for coffee, and generally living on your time. Once the baby arrives, your world gets a lot smaller, and it’s often just you and the baby following the same routine day in and day out.

“Feeling trapped in one's house or apartment … can just really amplify the stuckness of the mood,” says Monk. Plus, if you’re already in the thick of PPD, getting out of the house, or even off the couch, can feel impossible.

But even the littlest of wins can make a big impact on how you feel, says Monk. This isn’t about uprooting your life or your comfort zone. A small change of scenery can do wonders to improve your mood.

You know how a smell can take you back to your grandmother’s kitchen? The same can happen with certain environments. Memory research has long shown that the brain connects memories with places, and memories bring emotions with them, says Monk. Now picture a new mom whose whole day happens in the same couple of rooms (probably covered with burp cloths, diapers, and breast pads). It makes sense that emotions would get tangled up in those surroundings.

Taking care of a baby means routines come alongside chaos, says Monk. “People's worlds can start to feel centered in maybe the bedroom or a baby's room or the living room,” she says. “People can get quite planted and rooted.”

Science has also looked into whether how a home looks and feels can alter your mood. A 2011 study of about 2,100 mothers found that moms whose homes were crowded or noisy had slightly higher odds of screening positive for depression. A small UCLA study in 2010 also showed that women who described their homes as cluttered and full of unfinished projects reported feeling down as the day went on, while those who described restful, relaxing spaces reported feeling less down.

A natural solution for getting out of the house is going outside, and it works. Spending time in nature, whether that’s hiking a trail or simply taking in the scenery, could help you feel better, says Gina South, M.D., M.S., associate professor of emergency medicine at Penn Medicine, who studies how nature affects mental health.

“There is something very specific about nature that we connect to at a very deep level that impacts our brains and our experience,” says South.

One reason lies in something called fractals, or repeating geometric patterns found organically in nature. Consider a tree: The trunk splits into big branches, which split into smaller branches, which split into twigs, and those twigs split into leaves with leaf veins — all those splits follow a similar pattern.

Research shows our brains can process these patterns with little effort, which may ease mental fatigue, reduce psychological stress, and improve attention, says South. In fact, a 2015 study found that healthy adults who took a single 90-minute nature walk showed lower activity in the region of the brain associated with rumination than those who walked just as long on a busy road.

In her own randomized controlled trial, South and her co-authors surveyed the mental health of residents living near vacant lots in Philadelphia before and after some of these lots were planted with grass and trees. Those living near the new green spaces reported fewer feelings of depression and worthlessness than those near the untouched areas. “It showed that if you change the environment, it could change the trajectory of someone's mental health,” she says.

Getting outside is also associated with socialization and physical activity, both of which have been shown to improve mood, says South. “Those social connections are very important for mental health, for depression, including for postpartum depression where people can feel isolated and [that they have] low social support,” she says.

So what exactly counts as “being in nature”? It can be taking a walk by a green space, sitting at a park bench, going to a nearby lake, or even as simple as stepping out to your backyard for five minutes.

“Include nature in your toolkit,” says South. “Going outside is not going to prevent [or treat] depression, so it’s also important to talk to your physician. It's so hard to change behavior; it's so hard sometimes to get out of a rut, but start small.”

Even if you desperately want to get out of the house, planning an outing with a newborn — even if it’s just a walk around the block — can be overwhelming. If the thought of getting outside paralyzes you with worries about blowouts and meltdowns, there are ways to change your environment without leaving home.

Create a list of things that please you, even if they seem silly or insignificant, suggests Monk. They can be as simple as drinking tea in a special mug, eating a meal at the dining table instead of the couch, taking 15 minutes to call a friend, feeding your baby in a different room, or lighting your favorite candle. Small actions can break up your routine and remind you this stage isn’t forever, she says.

If you feel like you have nowhere to escape in your own home, just taking a step to transport your mind can help shift your mood, says Monk. This can look like opening up a book, streaming a favorite TV show, listening to music or a podcast, she says. These are “things that can both be distracting [and] focus the mind elsewhere but are taking an action,” she says. “That underscores, ‘Oh, I can do things to help myself feel better.’”

Determined not to feel trapped again, Seabrook created a place that she could call her own when she was pregnant with her second child. She transformed her screened-in back porch into a colorful, cozy oasis, which served as a visible reminder that she was going to be OK, she explains.

“That was my safe space,” she says. “I had a scheduled C-section, and I knew when we were going to the hospital that morning that I had that [space] to come home to no matter how bad it got.” She didn’t experience PPD with her second birth, but that porch still became her favorite place in the house.

This tactic has now become her go-to advice for postpartum moms who feel boxed in. Simply put: Claim a spot, she says.

“And it needs to be clear of baby stuff …. It doesn't have to be a big spot. It could be a chair,” says Seabrook. “If there is enough room, make it a room. You're worth that. Who you were, who you are now, and who you are going to become — you need space for all of that.”
